b: Hot take: All crowd-pleasing Shakespeare is good Shakespeare. If Marvel celebrities, mid-show Backstreet Boys sing-alongs, and confetti cannons help entice audiences to show up and lean into Much Ado About Nothing without trepidation, that’s theater worth making. In the big picture, then, the value of Jamie Lloyd’s Much Ado About Nothing, gaudy and glossy as it may be, lies less in its own artistry than in the giddy response of its audience.

But as far as Much Ado About Nothings go, Lloyd’s take is mid-tier. Unlike his Sunset Boulevard, this production has plenty of earnest love for the material but little appreciation for its emotional modulations. Much Ado About Nothing is the Bard’s cleverest comedy, the banter between Benedick (Tom Hiddleston) and Beatrice (Hayley Atwell) serving as the fount for the future champagne wit of Wilde and Coward. While Benedick’s war buddy Claudio (James Phoon) swiftly woos Beatrice’s cousin Hero (Mara Huf), all their friends conspire to drag Benedick and Beatrice kicking and screaming down the enemies-to-lovers highway.

“I was born to speak all mirth and no matter,” Beatrice says, and Benedick’s friend Don Pedro (Gerald Kyd) claims that “from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot, he is all mirth.” Lloyd’s Much Ado About Nothing desperately wants to be all mirth as well. But for all its fun, and sometimes to Lloyd’s frustration, this is also a play about what happens when two people ruthlessly committed to the bit finally have to grow up to get what they want.

Lloyd’s central conceit here is “party.” Ushers dance in the aisles throughout the preshow and intermission, instigating the wave multiple times and encouraging audience members to boogie with them like cringe bar mitzvah motivators. The set by Soutra Gilmour, Lloyd’s longtime collaborator, is bare except for a near-ceaseless downpour of pink confetti and a giant inflatable pink heart. Under Jon Clark’s pop-concert lighting, Hero’s sassy gentlewoman Margaret (Mason Alexander Park, London’s original Oh, Mary! star) keeps belting anthems with important pro-party messages like “(You Gotta) Fight for Your Right (To Party!).”

But after creating this jubilant atmosphere, Lloyd doesn’t have much variety in his directorial playlist. A fresh burst of confetti follows every dramatic moment, no matter its tone, turning Much Ado About Nothing’s first half into a festive haze with diminishing returns. Beatrice realizes she loves Benedick: confetti. Claudio thinks he sees Hero screwing someone else in her window: confetti. Hiddleston and Atwell finally make out: air horn…and confetti.

As in several of his star-driven productions, Lloyd blurs the line between character and A-list performer. It’s cute when Hiddleston encourages the women in the audience to cheer when Benedick tells Beatrice, “I am loved of all ladies”; we can recognize the meta-overlap between movie star and local legend. But when cardboard cutouts of the actors dressed as Loki and Peggy Carter, their Marvel roles, emerge, Lloyd is no longer attached to the world of the play. (It’s also becoming a tired signature: He did much the same thing with Nicole Scherzinger’s Pussycat Dolls reference in Sunset Boulevard and a Bill & Ted shout-out in Waiting for Godot.)

Fortunately, Atwell and Hiddleston are far from cardboard cutouts themselves. Hiddleston is a delightful physical clown, cavorting through the confetti mounds and buffoonishly body-rolling on the dance floor, and he conveys both Benedick’s outward suaveness and his pitiable self-doubt, as if his contempt for Beatrice stems from disbelief that she could ever care for him. The two share a crackling rapport, even if they’re so obviously flirty from the jump that you never quite believe they could deeply hurt each other. But when Beatrice tells Benedick to avenge her cousin’s honor, to use his hand “for my love some other way than swearing by it,” Atwell gets a sudden silver glint in her eye, a superpower all Beatrice’s own, and Benedick shrinks from it.

Lloyd’s usual trick, in which actors sit in plastic chairs and deliver their lines facing forward with minimal blocking, may not be the best fit for Shakespeare, even though it’s a technique designed to zero in on the text. Cogent contemporary Shakespeare performance relies on a lot more than the sound of line readings; without the elucidative context of fully realized gesture or lived-in physical worlds, portions of the poetry come across as approximate here. (Kenny Leon’s near-definitive 2019 production for Shakespeare in the Park set a high bar for razor-sharp clarity.)

Lloyd also can’t sustain momentum in the moodier, speechier second half of the production, which swaps biting prose for lengthy verse once Claudio abandons Hero at the altar; the necessary tonal shift seems an inconvenience in a production so fervently devoted to a good time. His one real stroke of reinterpretation comes earlier, right before intermission. The back-to-back scenes in which Benedick and Beatrice are conned into believing that the other is in love with them typically play as twin sequences: In most productions, physical hilarity ensues as each tries to avoid being caught eavesdropping. Lloyd and Hiddleston pull out all the stops for Benedick’s scene, in which he buries himself in confetti and rolls around in it.

But Beatrice’s scene is shockingly quiet. She listens, totally still, to Hero and Margaret’s critique: “Her wit values itself so highly that to her/All matter else seems weak,” Hero explains, knowing her cousin is listening. “She is so self-endeared.” Atwell’s Beatrice gets a spotlit moment most Beatrices don’t, of hearing herself anatomized by those closest to her, of meeting herself behind the mirthful mask. But the briefly moving moment passes in a new torrent of confetti, and it’s impossible to tell through all that pink just what it is that she sees.
Much Ado About Nothing is now running at the Winter Garden Theatre.
